1. Global Homicide Rate Overview

Between 1990 and 2023, the global intentional homicide landscape has shown a modest long-term decline in median rates, though progress has been uneven and partially masked by shifting country coverage. The global median rate — a robust measure less sensitive to outliers — has trended downward from around 3.4 per 100,000 in 1990 to 1.84 per 100,000 in 2023, suggesting that the typical country has become safer.

However, the global mean rate is more volatile, driven by a small number of extremely high-rate countries (notably in Latin America and the Caribbean). Mean rates peaked in the mid-1990s at approximately 9.7 per 100,000, declined through the 2000s and 2010s, and have hovered around 7–8 per 100,000 since 2015. The divergence between median and mean underscores the persistent influence of outliers.

Key insight: The world is becoming safer for the median country, but extreme violence in a concentrated set of nations continues to elevate the global average. Policy attention must therefore balance broad prevention with targeted interventions in outlier jurisdictions.

2. Regional & Country-Level Comparison

Geographic disparities in homicide rates are stark. In 2023, Latin America & the Caribbean recorded a regional mean of 28.0 per 100,000 — roughly 26 times higher than Europe’s mean of 1.1. North America and South America also posted elevated means, while Asia, Oceania, and Europe clustered at the lower end of the distribution.

Over the decades, divergent trajectories emerge. Latin America & the Caribbean has seen a worsening trend (from ~10.6 in the 1990s to ~25.0 in the 2020s), while South America has improved markedly (from ~24.5 to ~12.9). Europe and Asia have recorded consistent, sustained declines.

Country Outliers (2023)

The highest national rate in 2023 was Saint Kitts and Nevis at 64.2 per 100,000 — more than 900× the rate of Singapore (0.07). Among the bottom ten, several European and East Asian jurisdictions report rates below 0.6, reflecting highly effective public safety systems.

3. Gender Disparity in Homicide Victimization

One of the most pronounced findings in the UNODC data is the extraordinary gender gap in homicide victimization. Globally, the median male-to-female homicide rate ratio stands at 3.2:1, meaning that in the typical reporting country, males are killed at more than triple the rate of females. The mean ratio is even higher (~5.7:1), driven by countries where male victimization reaches extreme levels.

Over time, the ratio has remained relatively stable, fluctuating between roughly 2.9 and 3.5 since 2014. Both male and female mean rates declined from 2016–2020 before ticking upward again in 2021–2023. This synchronous movement suggests that macro-level factors (economic stress, conflict, policing capacity) affect both sexes, even if the absolute burden falls disproportionately on men.

Disaggregated prevention strategies — community-based violence reduction for young men and targeted domestic-violence interventions for women — are both warranted.

4. Age Group Analysis

When data are disaggregated by age, young adults emerge as the most at-risk demographic. The 25–29 age group records the highest mean homicide rate (29.4 for males, 3.2 for females), followed closely by 20–24 and 18–19. Risk declines steadily with age, with the 60+ group experiencing roughly one-third the male rate of the 25–29 cohort.

The male-to-female ratio is most extreme in the prime young-adult years (25–29 ratio: 9.1:1), narrowing for children and the elderly. This pattern is consistent with criminological evidence that young men are disproportionately involved in both offending and victimization related to street violence, organized crime, and gang activity.

Conversely, El Salvador’s decline from 134.3 to 7.9 represents one of the most remarkable turnarounds in global public safety, likely reflecting post-conflict stabilization and targeted gang-intervention policies.

6. Data Limitations & Policy Recommendations

Data Limitations

This analysis is subject to important caveats that affect interpretation:

  • Unbalanced panel: Not all countries report data for every year. Coverage peaked at 162 countries (2008) but fell to only 84 countries (2023) — just 41.8% of the 201 jurisdictions in the dataset. Year-to-year changes in the mean rate partly reflect who is reporting, not only what is happening.
  • Missing data are not interpolated: Gaps are left as absent rows. Analysts should avoid treating the global mean as a true population-weighted world average; it is an average of reporting countries only.
  • United Kingdom caveat: UK data refer to England and Wales only. Scotland and Northern Ireland are reported separately where available.
  • Territories: Some territories (e.g., Hong Kong, Puerto Rico) appear as distinct entries and should not be double-counted with parent states.

Policy Recommendations

Based on the evidence presented, the following actions are recommended for policy analysts and public safety stakeholders:

  1. Target Latin America & the Caribbean: The region’s rising decade-over-decade mean and concentration of outlier countries demand intensified international cooperation on violence prevention, judicial reform, and community policing.
  2. Invest in youth-focused interventions: The 18–29 age bracket bears the highest victimization burden. Programs targeting at-risk young men — employment, mentorship, and gang-exit pathways — offer high leverage.
  3. Maintain gender-disaggregated monitoring: The 3:1 to 6:1 male-to-female ratio is a critical KPI. Countries should collect and publish sex-disaggregated data routinely to ensure prevention resources match victimization patterns.
  4. Learn from success stories: El Salvador, Singapore, Hong Kong, and Italy demonstrate that dramatic reductions are achievable. Systematic case-study research into institutional and policy drivers of these declines should be prioritized.
  5. Strengthen global reporting infrastructure: With coverage falling below 42% in 2023, the international community must support national statistical and criminal-justice systems in low-capacity countries to close data gaps.
